lessonTitle: Subcooling, Two-Stage Cycles and Refrigerant Choice

blocks.text: A cold-chain warehouse in a hot climate runs its refrigeration plant with a condensing temperature of 45 °C and an evaporating temperature of -30 °C. A single compressor would have to work across a pressure ratio near 10, and it would overheat. Engineers fix this with simple tweaks: subcool the liquid, split the compression into two stages, and choose the refrigerant to suit the duty.

blocks.markdown: The ideal cycle from the previous unit is only a starting point. Real plants add **subcooling** (cooling the liquid below its saturation temperature after the condenser), **superheating** (heating the vapour above saturation leaving the evaporator) and sometimes **two-stage compression**. Each change alters the refrigerating effect $q_L$ and the compressor work $w_{in}$, so each changes the COP $= q_L / w_{in}$.

blocks.title: Subcooling and superheating
blocks.text: Subcooling: liquid leaves the condenser at a temperature below $T_{sat}(P_{cond})$, so $h_3$ is lower than $h_f$. Superheating: vapour leaves the evaporator at a temperature above $T_{sat}(P_{evap})$, so $h_1$ is higher than $h_g$. Superheat guarantees dry vapour at the compressor inlet.

blocks.caption: Liquid-state enthalpy approximated by the saturated liquid value at the actual liquid temperature; $c_{p,l}$ is the liquid specific heat (kJ/kg K).

blocks.markdown: Subcooling lowers $h_3$, and because the valve is isenthalpic, $h_4 = h_3$ is lower too. That makes the refrigerating effect $h_1 - h_4$ **larger** while compressor work $h_2 - h_1$ is unchanged. COP therefore rises, at no cost in compressor power. Superheating in the cold space also adds to $q_L$, but the vapour has a larger specific volume, so compressor work per kg rises; the net COP effect depends on the refrigerant, and the main reason for superheat is to keep liquid out of the compressor.

blocks.title: Effect of subcooling on COP
blocks.prompt: An ideal cycle has $h_1 = 240.0$ kJ/kg, $h_2 = 275.0$ kJ/kg and condenser exit saturated liquid $h_3 = 100.0$ kJ/kg. Liquid is then subcooled so that $h_3 = 92.0$ kJ/kg. Assume $h_1$ and $h_2$ are unchanged (typical, approximate data). Find the COP before and after and the percentage change.

steps.text: With subcooling: $h_4 = 92.0$, so $q_L = 240.0 - 92.0 = 148.0$ kJ/kg; work is unchanged.

blocks.answer: COP rises from 4.000 to 4.229, an increase of 5.7%.

blocks.title: Why two stages?
blocks.text: At large pressure ratios a single stage gives high discharge temperature, low volumetric efficiency and large work. In a two-stage cycle with **flash intercooling**, a flash chamber at an intermediate pressure separates the vapour formed on the first throttle. That vapour bypasses the evaporator and is mixed into the low-pressure compressor discharge, so the evaporator carries only liquid, the low-pressure compressor handles less flow and the high-pressure compressor receives cooled vapour.

blocks.latex: x = \frac{h_5 - h_f}{h_g - h_f} \qquad \dot m_{LP} = \frac{\dot Q_L}{h_1 - h_{f}} \qquad \dot m_{HP} = \frac{\dot m_{LP}}{1 - x}
blocks.caption: Flash chamber: $h_5$ = enthalpy of liquid after the first valve (= condenser liquid), $h_f,\,h_g$ at the intermediate pressure; $x$ = mass fraction of the HP flow that flashes.

blocks.title: Flash chamber mass fractions
blocks.prompt: A two-stage cycle with a flash chamber removes a 10 kW load. Representative data for the working fluid: condenser liquid $h_5 = 110.0$ kJ/kg; at the intermediate pressure $h_f = 80.0$ kJ/kg, $h_g = 237.0$ kJ/kg; evaporator exit $h_1 = 230.0$ kJ/kg. Liquid from the chamber is throttled to the evaporator, so $h_8 = h_f$. Find the flash fraction and the mass flow through each compressor stage.

steps.text: The first valve is isenthalpic, so the mixture in the chamber has $h = 110.0$ kJ/kg. Quality is found from lever rule.
The evaporator carries liquid from the chamber: $q_L = h_1 - h_8 = 230.0 - 80.0 = 150.0$ kJ/kg.
Only $(1-x)$ of the HP flow is liquid leaving the chamber.

blocks.answer: Flash fraction x = 0.1911; LP compressor flow 0.0667 kg/s; HP compressor flow 0.0824 kg/s.

rows: ODP 0, GWP about 1400, non-toxic, non-flammable; moderate pressures
ODP 0, GWP 0, very high latent heat, toxic and mildly flammable; industrial plants
ODP 0, GWP about 3, highly flammable; small charge systems
ODP 0, GWP 1, non-toxic, very high pressures; often transcritical
ODP about 0.05, GWP about 1800; phased out under the Montreal Protocol
blocks.caption: Typical, approximate refrigerant data used for comparison; consult property tables for design.

blocks.markdown: Large latent heat means less mass flow for the same load, so smaller piping and compressors. Pressure levels matter: too low an evaporator pressure (below atmosphere) allows air in; too high a condenser pressure needs thick-walled equipment. Environmental indicators are the ozone depletion potential (ODP) and the global warming potential (GWP), both relative to a reference substance (CFC-11 and CO2 respectively).

items: Pick evaporator pressure above atmospheric to avoid air leaking in.
Pick condenser pressure low enough for economic pipework.
High latent heat reduces mass flow and equipment size.
Zero ODP and low GWP for compliance; weigh against toxicity and flammability.

blocks.title: Trade-offs, not a single best fluid
blocks.text: Ammonia has the best thermodynamic properties but is toxic; propane is efficient and cheap but flammable; CO2 is benign but runs at very high pressure with lower efficiency in hot climates. Safety class matters as much as COP.

points: Subcooling raises refrigerating effect at constant compressor work, so COP rises.
Superheating protects the compressor; its COP effect depends on the fluid.
Flash intercooling in two-stage cycles suits large pressure ratios: lower compressor work, lower discharge temperature, lower evaporator flow.
Refrigerants are compared on pressure levels, latent heat, ODP, GWP, toxicity and flammability.

questions.stem: A liquid-line subcooler lowers the temperature of liquid leaving the condenser while the compressor operating conditions stay the same. What is the effect on COP?

options.text: Compressor work increases, so COP decreases
Refrigerating effect decreases because the liquid is colder
The refrigerating effect increases while compressor work is unchanged, so COP increases
COP is unchanged because the same refrigerant circulates

questions.correctOptionText: The refrigerating effect increases while compressor work is unchanged, so COP increases

distractorRationale.a: Compressor work depends on $h_2 - h_1$, which is unchanged.
distractorRationale.b: Colder liquid has lower $h_3 = h_4$, so $h_1 - h_4$ is larger.
distractorRationale.d: The refrigerating effect changes, so COP changes.

questions.explanation: Subcooling lowers $h_3$, and $h_4 = h_3$ for the isenthalpic valve. The evaporator then absorbs $h_1 - h_4$, which is larger, with the same compressor work.

questions.stem: For a given cooling load, which refrigerant property most directly reduces the required mass flow rate?

options.text: A large latent heat of vaporisation
A high critical temperature
A low normal boiling point
A high ODP

questions.correctOptionText: A large latent heat of vaporisation

distractorRationale.b: Critical temperature affects cycle shape, not directly mass flow per kW.
distractorRationale.c: Boiling point sets pressure levels, not mass flow per kW.
distractorRationale.d: ODP is an environmental measure unrelated to flow rate.

questions.explanation: Mass flow is $\dot m = \dot Q_L / q_L$, and $q_L$ is mainly the latent heat absorbed during boiling. A larger latent heat means fewer kilograms are needed, so ammonia plants need smaller lines than R-134a plants.

questions.stem: Why is a two-stage cycle with flash intercooling attractive for a large pressure ratio such as an evaporator at -30 °C and a condenser at 45 °C?

options.text: It eliminates the need for a throttling valve
It raises the refrigerating effect by compressing the vapour isentropically at the evaporator pressure
It lets the condenser operate at a lower temperature than the surroundings
It cuts total compressor work and discharge temperature and removes flash vapour before the evaporator

questions.correctOptionText: It cuts total compressor work and discharge temperature and removes flash vapour before the evaporator

distractorRationale.a: Two valves are still used; flash intercooling adds one.
distractorRationale.b: Compression occurs in two stages; the evaporator pressure is not changed this way.
distractorRationale.c: The condenser must remain above the sink temperature.

questions.explanation: Splitting compression with an intermediate cooling step reduces the work for a given overall pressure ratio and keeps discharge temperature down. The flash chamber also passes the flashed vapour straight to the HP compressor instead of letting it circulate through the evaporator.

questions.stem: A designer for a large cold store wants a working fluid with zero ODP, near-zero GWP and very high latent heat, and the plant is staffed and ventilated for toxic gas. Which refrigerant best fits?

options.text: Ammonia (R-717)
A legacy CFC

distractorRationale.a: ODP above zero and phased out under the Montreal Protocol.
distractorRationale.c: GWP of about 1400 and much lower latent heat than ammonia.
distractorRationale.d: High ODP and banned for new equipment.

questions.explanation: Ammonia has zero ODP, GWP of 0 and a latent heat of about 1370 kJ/kg, several times that of halocarbons. Its toxicity is accepted in industrial plants with proper safety systems.

questions.stem: The vapour leaving an evaporator is superheated by 5 K in the cold space before reaching the compressor. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It always lowers compressor work because the vapour is warmer
It has no effect on either refrigerating effect or work
It adds to the refrigerating effect and ensures no liquid enters the compressor, but the larger specific volume increases compressor work per kg
It reduces the refrigerating effect because less vapour is saturated

questions.correctOptionText: It adds to the refrigerating effect and ensures no liquid enters the compressor, but the larger specific volume increases compressor work per kg

distractorRationale.a: Warmer vapour has a larger specific volume, so compression work per kg increases.
distractorRationale.d: The extra enthalpy absorbed in the cold space adds to the refrigerating effect.

questions.explanation: Superheat raises $h_1$ and so increases $q_L$ if the heat comes from the cold space. The vapour also has a larger specific volume, raising $w_{in}$, so the net COP change depends on the fluid. Its key role is protecting the compressor from liquid slugging.

questions.stem: A refrigerant liquid leaves the condenser at saturation and is subcooled by 7 K. Assume liquid specific heat $c_{p,l} = 1.4$ kJ/(kg K), constant. By how much does the refrigerating effect increase, in kJ/kg?
questions.explanation: Subcooling lowers $h_3$, and so $h_4$, by $c_{p,l}\Delta T = 1.4 \times 7 = 9.8$ kJ/kg. Since $h_1$ is unchanged, the refrigerating effect $h_1 - h_4$ rises by the same amount.

questions.stem: A chiller has $h_1 = 250.0$ kJ/kg, $h_2 = 290.0$ kJ/kg and condenser-exit liquid $h_3 = 120.0$ kJ/kg. Fitting a subcooler reduces $h_3$ to 108.0 kJ/kg without changing $h_1$ or $h_2$. Calculate the percentage increase in COP.

A two-stage plant with a flash chamber serves a load of 6.0 kW. Data for the refrigerant: liquid from the condenser $h = 118.0$ kJ/kg; at the intermediate pressure $h_f = 84.0$ kJ/kg and $h_g = 240.0$ kJ/kg; evaporator exit $h_1 = 236.0$ kJ/kg; chamber liquid is throttled to the evaporator. Find the mass flow rate through the high-pressure compressor in kg/s.

A plant engineer must choose between R-134a, ammonia and propane for three installations: (i) a small domestic fridge, (ii) a large cold store with trained staff and (iii) a mid-size supermarket chiller in a public space. Justify a suitable choice for each using pressure level, latent heat, safety and environmental impact.
markingGuide: Domestic: propane (R-290) with a very small charge or a halocarbon; low GWP, flammability limited by small charge
Cold store: ammonia; very high latent heat, ODP and GWP of zero, toxicity managed by trained staff
Supermarket: low-charge or secondary loop with a non-toxic fluid, or R-134a replacement with low GWP, because the public is nearby
Mentions latent heat sets mass flow and equipment size
Mentions ODP and GWP of the options
questions.explanation: No refrigerant is best everywhere. Latent heat, pressure levels, safety class, charge size and environmental indices (ODP, GWP) are weighed together, and the choice differs by application.

questions.stem: A refrigerator evaporates at 0.12 MPa and condenses at 1.2 MPa. Show that a single stage has a pressure ratio of 10 and estimate the intermediate pressure for a two-stage cycle with equal stage pressure ratios. Explain, with reference to flash intercooling, why the two-stage cycle uses less work and gives a safer discharge temperature.
markingGuide: Equal ratios give intermediate pressure $\sqrt{0.12 \times 1.2} = 0.379$ MPa and a ratio of about 3.16 per stage
Work for gas compression is roughly minimised when each stage has the same ratio
Flash chamber removes vapour formed in the first throttle so it is not compressed from the low pressure
Vapour entering the HP compressor is cooled by mixing with the flash vapour, reducing discharge temperature
Evaporator carries only liquid from the chamber, so more of its capacity is useful refrigeration
questions.explanation: The pressure ratio is 1.2/0.12 = 10, so each of two equal stages has ratio $\sqrt{10} = 3.16$ with intermediate pressure 0.379 MPa. Splitting the compression and cooling the vapour between stages cuts work and discharge temperature.
